title: How Career Centers Can Sustain Career Tool Engagement With Incentives
summary: Should students earn rewards for completing career activities, demonstrating improvement, or meeting readiness standards? Explore incentive models, qualification criteria, real university examples, and ways to encourage meaningful career tool engagement beyond initial participation.
body_markdown:
## How can career centers use incentives to sustain career tool engagement?


Career centers can use incentives when students start career activities but do not complete meaningful next steps. Effective incentives should reward improvement, readiness, or continued preparation, not just logins or activity counts, while preserving fair access for students with different schedules and starting points.


If your career center is considering incentives to encourage students to keep using career tools, deciding what students must accomplish to earn those rewards can be more complicated than choosing the rewards themselves.


While badges, certificates, and other forms of recognition may encourage participation, fixed activity requirements, readiness thresholds, and eligibility-based rewards can create unintended challenges for students at different stages of preparation.


This guide examines which incentive models are worth considering, how to set fair qualification criteria with examples from existing university recognition programs and ways to discourage score-chasing while encouraging continued career preparation beyond the reward.


## Should Career Centers Offer Incentives for Continued Career Tool Use?


Career centers should consider incentives when students begin career preparation activities but do not complete the steps needed to benefit from them. The decision should depend on where participation drops off, what additional action students need to take, and whether recognition would encourage that action without creating unnecessary work for students or counselors.


While[student ambassador-led tool activation](https://www.hiration.com/blog/student-ambassadors-career-tool-adoption-guide-higher-ed/) can help students complete their first platform action, incentives address a different challenge: getting them to return and follow through.


For example, if students regularly complete an initial resume review but rarely make revisions, a completion-based incentive might help.


And if students already revise their resumes independently, introducing a reward may add little value.


This approach also aligns with the[NACE Career Readiness Competencies](https://www.hiration.com/blog/nace-career-readiness-competencies-guide-higher-ed/) , which emphasize demonstrated competencies rather than participation alone.


### Which incentive models are worth considering?


Different incentives serve different purposes, and choosing the wrong one can create more administrative work than the engagement it generates.


Incentive model When it makes sense What students should complete


Readiness badges Recognizing progress in a specific skill A defined preparation milestone supported by assessment evidence


Certificates Recognizing a broader preparation pathway Multiple activities with reflection or assessment


Course credit Connecting optional career preparation to academic learning Faculty-approved activities that meet academic requirements


Recognition Acknowledging meaningful effort or improvement A documented achievement or improvement milestone


Program/event eligibility Preparing students for a specific optional opportunity Relevant preparation demonstrated through accessible criteria


Completion milestones Encouraging students to finish work they have started A complete feedback, revision, or practice cycle


Small rewards Encouraging participation in a short, targeted challenge A substantive activity with clear completion criteria


These models also involve different trade-offs.


A readiness badge may be suitable for a resume improvement challenge because students can complete the activity independently and counselors can define consistent standards.


Course credit requires faculty involvement and alignment with academic policies. It may work for optional,[credit-bearing career development activities](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-assignments-curriculum-integration-higher-ed/) , but should not become a requirement for accessing existing career technology.


[Event eligibility](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-treks-student-engagement/) requires additional care. Offering an optional networking opportunity to students who complete relevant preparation is different from restricting access to general career services.


Career centers should also consider the timing of rewards. A small incentive offered after an initial review may encourage students to finish one task, while a certificate awarded after several meaningful activities can recognize preparation across a longer period.


The most useful starting point is the activity students are abandoning, not the reward the career center wants to introduce.


What to reward across five career preparation activities


## Which Student Behaviors Should Career Centers Incentivize?


Career centers should prioritize activities that require students to act on previous feedback, demonstrate improvement, or complete a meaningful next step. Rather than reward every platform interaction, incentive criteria should identify what qualifies as a completed preparation activity and how that achievement can be assessed consistently across students with different starting points.


Career activity Weak qualification criterion Stronger qualification criterion


Resume building Uploading a resume multiple times Completing a revision based on feedback and meeting agreed criteria


Mock interviews Completing five practice sessions Reviewing feedback and demonstrating improvement in a subsequent attempt


LinkedIn optimization Repeatedly using the optimization tool Revising relevant sections against an established checklist


Career exploration Completing several assessments Comparing suitable career options and documenting a justified next step


Cover letters Generating multiple drafts Revising one letter for a target opportunity using specific feedback


### Reward completed improvement cycles


Consider a student whose first resume review identifies weak accomplishment statements and limited alignment with their target role.


Instead of offering a reward for another submission, the career center could establish the following completion criteria:


1. **Review:** Identify two or three priority improvements from the initial feedback.
2. **Revise:** Update the relevant sections rather than generating an entirely new resume unnecessarily.
3. **Reassess:** Submit the revised document and check whether the identified weaknesses have been addressed.
4. **Demonstrate readiness:** Meet an agreed standard or provide evidence of meaningful improvement.


This distinction also applies to mock interviews.


A student who completes five practice sessions without addressing recurring weaknesses should not automatically qualify for a higher-level recognition than someone who completes two sessions and demonstrates substantial improvement.


However, requiring additional attempts from students who already meet the expected standard can create unnecessary work.


Career centers could allow those students to qualify through an appropriate readiness assessment rather than requiring revisions solely to satisfy an activity count.


### Make room for improvement, not just high performance


One difficult decision is whether students should receive recognition for meeting a fixed readiness threshold or for improving from their starting point.


Using only a fixed threshold can disadvantage students who need more preparation. Rewarding improvement alone, without defining its significance, can make recognition inconsistent.


Career centers can address this through two distinct milestones:


- **Improvement milestone:** Awarded when a student completes a meaningful revision or practice cycle and demonstrates progress against defined criteria.
- **Readiness milestone:** Awarded when a student demonstrates the established standard for a particular career preparation activity.


These milestones should have different meanings. An improvement badge should recognize development without implying that the student has already achieved the final readiness standard.


Career centers also need to decide how to handle students who begin above the readiness threshold. Those students should not be required to weaken or repeatedly revise already-strong materials to qualify for recognition.


**A further consideration is what happens after the milestone is earned.**


For example, a career center running a voluntary resume improvement challenge could examine whether participants subsequently return to practice interviews, update their resumes for new opportunities, or complete another relevant activity without an additional reward.


[Tracking meaningful activity over a defined period](https://www.hiration.com/blog/career-center-dashboard-best-practices-higher-ed/) , such as 30 to 60 days after recognition, would provide a more useful picture of continued engagement than counting how many badges were awarded.


This period is an illustrative evaluation choice, not a universal benchmark.


## What Can Career Centers Learn From Existing University Incentive Programs?


University programs demonstrate several approaches to recognizing career preparation, including tiered activity completion, assessed learning, and evidence-based credentials. Their structures offer useful design lessons, but they also raise questions about whether completing more activities means students are better prepared and whether participation continues after rewards have been earned.


### Georgia Tech: Tiered rewards for career preparation


Georgia Institute of Technology's[Jacket Job Ready Challenge](https://career.gatech.edu/jacketjobready/?ref=hiration.com) allows students to earn recognition through career development activities.


Students progress through three achievement levels:


- Bronze: 5 activities
- Silver: 10 activities
- Gold: 15 activities


Eligible activities include workshops, networking events, recorded mock interviews, career treks, and other designated career preparation experiences.


The program also provides tangible benefits. Silver-level participants can receive 15-minute early access to the All-Majors Career Fair, while Gold-level participants can receive 30-minute early access, subject to program requirements.


**What career centers can adapt:**


Georgia Tech's model demonstrates how progressive milestones and increasingly valuable rewards can be incorporated into a career preparation program.


However, the activity thresholds also raise an important design question: does completing fifteen activities necessarily demonstrate greater readiness than completing five?


A career center adapting this model specifically for career technology could retain the tiered structure while introducing additional evidence requirements at each level.


For instance, completing one mock interview might count toward an initial milestone, while a higher milestone could require students to review their feedback, complete a second attempt, and demonstrate improvement.


The program's early career fair access also illustrates why rewards tied to employer opportunities deserve careful consideration.


Career centers should examine whether eligibility criteria are accessible to students with different schedules, responsibilities, and preparation needs.


### Texas A&M University: Badges tied to structured learning


The Texas A&M University Career Center offered a[Career Readiness Bootcamp Badge program](https://careercenter.tamu.edu/events-and-programs/career-readiness-bootcamp-badge/?ref=hiration.com) from July 7 to August 7, 2026.


The program combined Canvas learning modules, career-focused workshops, reflections, assignments, and pre and post assessments.


Participants were required to complete three designated workshops and select two additional workshops. Students who met the program requirements could earn a digital badge to display on LinkedIn, resumes, or portfolios.


**What career centers can adapt:**


Unlike an incentive based on a single activity, this model combines structured learning with assessment and student choice.


Career centers could apply a similar approach to career technology by creating a voluntary preparation pathway in which students complete an initial assessment, undertake relevant practice, and demonstrate what has changed.


The pre and post assessment structure is particularly useful because it creates an opportunity to examine improvement rather than relying exclusively on activity completion.


However, earning a badge marks the end of the program requirements. It does not establish whether students continue preparing afterward.


A career center adapting this model could examine whether badge recipients subsequently use other relevant career resources without another incentive.


### Purdue University: Credentials supported by evidence


An[EDUCAUSE overview of Purdue University's Passport initiative](https://library.educause.edu/resources/2013/1/digital-badges-as-an-open-passport-for-learning?ref=hiration.com) , published in 2013, describes an approach in which instructors created online learning challenges and students could select different ways to complete them.


Instructors monitored progress and assessed student work, while digital badges represented achievements supported by evidence.


Although this was a broader educational credentialing initiative rather than a career center incentive program, its design offers a relevant lesson.


**What career centers can adapt:**


Allow students to demonstrate the same competency through different relevant activities instead of requiring everyone to follow an identical sequence.


For example, students pursuing a resume readiness milestone might qualify through an assessed resume revision or an advisor-reviewed submission, provided both routes use comparable criteria.


This flexibility can accommodate different levels of preparation and reduce unnecessary platform activity.


The challenge is maintaining consistency. Career centers need a shared standard that explains what counts as sufficient evidence, regardless of the route a student chooses.


Across these three examples, the key distinction is between **recognizing participation, assessing achievement, and encouraging continued preparation** .


An incentive program can accomplish the first two without necessarily achieving the third. Career centers should determine which outcome they are trying to influence before adapting any particular model.


Five principles for designing incentives that encourage lasting engagement


## How Can Career Centers Prevent Students From Chasing Rewards Instead of Readiness?


Career centers can reduce reward-driven behavior by separating activity completion from demonstrated readiness, setting achievable criteria for different student groups, and avoiding incentives that depend entirely on platform-generated scores. They should also evaluate whether students continue relevant preparation after recognition, rather than treating high participation or badge completion rates as sufficient evidence of success.


A[2023 systematic mapping study on the negative effects of gamification in educational software](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.08346?ref=hiration.com) identified reported problems involving points, badges, leaderboards, motivation, and students gaming incentive systems.


The findings do not mean career centers should avoid incentives altogether. They reinforce the need to examine how students might respond to the specific reward criteria being introduced.


### 1. Avoid making the highest AI score the ultimate achievement


AI-generated resume and interview scores can help students identify areas for improvement, but using those scores as the sole qualification criterion creates problems.


For example, students may repeatedly modify resume content to raise their scores without necessarily improving accuracy, relevance, or how effectively they communicate their experience.


Career centers should establish clear criteria for how platform scores contribute to recognition.


These might include:


- A minimum standard aligned with the specific preparation task
- Evidence that priority feedback has been addressed
- Accuracy and relevance of the final material
- Advisor review or an alternative assessment route when scores appear inconsistent


A particularly important decision is whether students must meet a threshold, demonstrate improvement, or satisfy both requirements.


These should be defined before the incentive launches. Otherwise, counselors may end up making inconsistent decisions about who qualifies.


### 2. Do not make students compete against one another


A leaderboard recognizing the ten highest resume scores can favor students who begin with stronger materials or have greater familiarity with professional recruitment.


Instead of ranking students against one another, career centers can recognize individual achievement against shared criteria.


For example, students could receive the same readiness badge for meeting the agreed standard, regardless of whether they required one review or several revision cycles.


Students who demonstrate substantial improvement but have not yet met that standard could receive a separate improvement milestone.


This allows recognition to reflect different achievements without implying they are equivalent.


### 3. Allow students to choose relevant activities


A single set of required platform activities may not serve students at different stages of career development.


A first-year student exploring possible careers may benefit from comparing occupational pathways and identifying next steps. A graduating student preparing for recruitment may need targeted resume feedback or interview practice.


Rather than creating one universal activity checklist, career centers could offer different voluntary milestone pathways.


The important design decision is how to make those pathways comparable.


Each should have a clearly defined outcome, evidence requirements, and completion criteria. Students should not have to complete unrelated activities simply to earn the same recognition as their peers.


### 4. Keep rewards proportional to the activity


Not every completed activity needs a certificate, prize, or new badge.


Small rewards may be appropriate for short preparation challenges, while substantial credentials should represent broader achievement or demonstrated competency.


Career centers should also consider whether introducing too many rewards creates an expectation that every subsequent activity will come with something in return.


One approach is to recognize larger milestones rather than individual platform actions.


For example, students might earn a certificate after completing a broader career preparation pathway, while individual resume revisions or interview attempts contribute toward that milestone without generating separate rewards.


This gives students a longer-term objective without attaching an incentive to every interaction.


### 5. Preserve access to essential career services


Eligibility-based incentives require particular care because some rewards affect access to valuable opportunities.


For example, priority entry to an employer event may appear to be a modest benefit, but it could advantage students who have more time to complete qualifying activities.


Career centers should examine three questions before connecting rewards to program access:


1. Can students reasonably meet the eligibility criteria regardless of their schedules or circumstances?
2. Is there an accessible alternative way to demonstrate the required preparation?
3. Does the incentive preserve ordinary access to essential career services and opportunities?


Optional recognition programs should not become indirect requirements for receiving support that students would otherwise be entitled to access.


Finally, career centers should assess what happens once students receive their rewards.


A practical evaluation can examine the proportion of participants who complete another meaningful activity without an additional incentive, the time between milestones, and whether assessed preparation improves.


These measures should be interpreted alongside participation patterns and student feedback. Higher completion rates alone do not establish that incentives caused sustained engagement.


The central decision for career centers is whether the program encourages useful preparation beyond the reward itself, or simply creates another activity target for students and staff to manage.


## Wrapping Up


Before expanding an incentive program, career centers should assess whether rewards reached previously disengaged students, accommodated different starting points, and encouraged continued preparation after they were earned.


These findings can help teams refine or retire incentives rather than introducing more rewards simply to maintain participation.

## Career Tool Incentives — FAQs


Should career centers offer incentives for career tool use?


Career centers should consider incentives when students begin preparation but do not complete the steps needed to benefit from the tool.


What student behaviors should incentives reward?


Incentives should reward meaningful actions such as revising after feedback, completing a preparation cycle, demonstrating improvement, or meeting a readiness standard.


Should incentives be based on activity counts?


Activity counts can be useful, but they should not be the only measure. Completing more activities does not always mean a student is better prepared.


How can career centers make incentives fair for different students?


Career centers can use separate improvement and readiness milestones so students are recognized for progress without forcing everyone through the same activity sequence.


What can career centers learn from university incentive programs?


Existing programs show how badges, tiered milestones, structured learning, assessments, and evidence-based credentials can recognize career preparation.


How can career centers prevent score-chasing?


Career centers should avoid making the highest AI score the main goal and instead combine scores with evidence of improvement, relevance, accuracy, and readiness.


Should rewards affect access to career services?


Incentives should not become indirect requirements for essential career support. Eligibility-based rewards need accessible criteria and alternative ways to qualify.
